title: Pip and the Wobbly Starfish

topics.value_lesson: trying again a different way is how learning works

spine: A small child learns that floating is not about holding on tight, but about letting the water hold you.

segments.text: The pool is quiet this morning. Just us, and Grandpa Joe, and the big basket of toys. Pip digs right to the bottom. "This one," says Pip. A bright yellow duck. "Dabble," says Grandpa Joe. "A fine name." On the shallow step, he pushes Dabble under. Blub. Up it pops. "Full of air," says Grandpa Joe. "That is why it floats." He hums his little bubble-tune. Pip watches Dabble bob. "I want to float like that," says Pip. "On my back." Grandpa Joe holds out his hands. Pip leans back. Lifts one foot. Lifts the other. Down goes Pip's bottom. Splash. "Ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe. Pip tries again. Feet up. Bottom down. Splash. "Ker-plop."

"Bubbles first," says Pip. Grandpa Joe hums his bubble-tune. Pip puts just their lips in the water. Blow. Blub-blub-blub. The bubbles tickle Pip's nose. It rumbles funny, like a purring cat. Pip giggles. Snort! Water goes up. "Too big," says Grandpa Joe. "Soft and slow, little fish." Pip tries again. Soft. Slow. Blub-blub-blub. A long stream of bubbles dances up. Then Pip takes a big breath. Their chest puffs up, round and full of air. Just like Dabble's round yellow belly. "Look," says Pip. "I'm full of air too." Grandpa Joe smiles. "That you are," he says. "That you are."

"Chase the duck," says Pip. Grandpa Joe tosses Dabble out. Ker-plop. Pip lies on their belly. Grandpa's hands hover close. Pip kicks stiff legs. Splash, splash. Nowhere. "Floppy feet," says Grandpa Joe. "Like a frog." Pip flops. Kick, kick, kick. The water pushes back. Pip scoots forward. One whole glide. The water holds Pip up the whole time. It feels like a big soft hand. Pip reaches. Gotcha. Dabble bobs in Pip's arms. "You floated," says Grandpa Joe. "On your belly." Pip hugs the wet yellow duck. "Again," says Pip. "Again."

Grandpa Joe turns Dabble upside down and pushes him under. Blub. Up he pops, right side up, bobbing. "Air inside," says Grandpa Joe. "That is the secret." He hums his little bubble-tune. Then he scrunches his hand into a ball. Down it dips, low in the water. He spreads his fingers wide, flat like a star. Up it floats. "See?" says Grandpa Joe. "Big breath. Loose body. Wide like a starfish." Pip looks at Dabble. Pip looks at the star-hand. "Like that?" says Pip. "Just like that," says Grandpa Joe. "Show me what you found." Pip takes a big, big breath. Arms out. Legs out. Grandpa Joe's warm hand rests under Pip's back. The water lifts. The water holds. Pip's feet leave the bottom. "I'm floating!" says Pip. "Ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe, softly. "No splash at all."

Pip takes a big breath. "One finger," says Grandpa Joe. Off comes one. "Two." Off comes two. Pip's cheeks puff out. Pip's toes wiggle above the water. Off comes the last finger, and Grandpa Joe's hand hovers close, not touching. The water lifts. The water holds. "I'm doing it!" says Pip. "All by myself!" Grandpa Joe hums his little bubble-tune. The lifeguard smiles and gives a thumbs-up. Dabble bobs beside them, bright and yellow. "Ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe, softly. "No splash at all." Then Pip stands up, laughing, and scoops Dabble close. Home they go, wrapped in the warm towel. And at bedtime, Dabble sits by Pip's pillow, ready for the story.

"Let's glide," says Pip. Grandpa Joe sets Dabble on the far step, bright and yellow, waiting. Pip leans back. Big breath. Arms out. Legs out. "One long, slow ker-plop," says Grandpa Joe. "Ready?" Pip kicks. Splash, splash, splash. The water lifts. The water holds. Pip glides on their back, right across the shallow step. "I'm moving!" says Pip. "I'm really moving!" Grandpa Joe hums his little bubble-tune, walking beside. Then — bump. Pip's fingers touch the step. "You made it!" says Grandpa Joe. Pip sits up, laughing, and grabs Dabble tight. Home they go, Dabble riding on Pip's tummy in the warm towel, still smelling of pool water.

choice_points.question: "Well, little fish, Dabble here floats easy as pie. Shall we practice our bubble-blowing first, or shall we chase this rascal duck across the water?"

choice_points.question: "You're floating, Pip, you're really floating! Now then — do you want to let go of my fingers one by one and float all by yourself, or shall we kick-glide on your back, nice and slow, all the way to Dabble?"

options.label: Let go one finger at a time and float solo
Kick-glide on your back across to the duck

gathered_but_unused: Your body is mostly water, and it can float if you lie still and take a big breath of air.
Blowing bubbles underwater tickles your nose and makes a funny rumbling sound.
Kicking your legs fast and splashy can push you forward through the water, even if your feet leave the bottom.
Some things float because they are full of air, like a rubber duck or an empty bucket turned upside down.
When you take a deep breath and hold it, your chest puffs up like a balloon and helps you float higher.
Water can hold you up if you spread your arms and legs out wide, like a star or a pancake.
If you scrunch up into a tight ball, you sink a little; if you stretch out long and flat, you float better.
Goggles help you see underwater, so you can watch your own bubbles and the grown-up’s hands nearby.
